fields.short: Maybe, but it hasn't been properly tested in people. In rats, a big dose killed 64 in 100 in a room not linked with heroin, and 32 in 100 in the heroin room.
how: The idea: the place, people and ritual that come with a drug start to trigger the body's push-back against it. That push-back is part of tolerance. So it may be weaker where the drug isn't usually taken.

In the rat study, each rat had heroin in one room and dummy injections of sugar water in the other. A big dose then killed about 64 in 100 rats in the dummy room, 32 in 100 in the heroin room, and 96 in 100 rats that had never had heroin.
Nobody measured the rats' tolerance, only whether they died. The paper also overstated how sure its result was, though more rats died in the dummy room in all six repeats. Rats aren't people.

In people, 10 survivors described the day they overdosed, on average 5 years later. 7 recalled something unusual: 3 a new place or crowd, 2 a different way of injecting, 2 a different mix of drugs. Nobody counted how often people use somewhere new with no overdose.

how: 17 published reports from clinics described 127 people with this damage. 126 had a hole in the septum, the wall between the nostrils. Fewer had damage further in: about 59 in 100 on the lower side walls, 30 in 100 in the roof of the mouth, 23 in 100 higher up, 8 in 100 at the eye socket or skull base. Most reports picked people with one kind of problem, so these shares are rough.

It can look like a disease that inflames blood vessels. In one Italian clinic, a blood test for that disease was positive in 13 of 18 people with cocaine damage, and some were first treated for that disease, which didn't help. Unlike many with that disease, none of the 18 had fever, weight loss, or joint, lung or ear problems when first seen.

None of these studies followed people after they stopped. In the Italian clinic, 4 people were scanned again months or years later. All 4 said they'd kept using cocaine, and all had more damage. In one, it reached the base of the skull within three years.

18 nose doctors agreed, as opinion, that stopping is the only known way to halt the damage. They said no amount of use is low enough to keep it from getting worse. They'd wait for drug tests showing 12 months off cocaine before repair surgery.

lines.reason: how 1: 'case series' is jargon, and the shares lacked the statement's caveat that 12 of 17 series picked people for one site or presentation (it can move the palate share). how 2: 'none had illness elsewhere in the body' is broader than the statement (fever, weight loss, joint, lung and ear signs were absent at presentation; CRP or ESR abnormal in about half; a lung abscess and eye-socket infections came later). how 3: 'had kept using' is their own report. how 4: 'no amount of use is safe for it' can read as being about anyone's nose; the panel said no amount keeps the lesions from progressing.

fields.short: About 5 in 100 people had an overdose treated by a doctor within 6 months of stopping, in US insurance records. Nearly half went to an emergency department.
how: US public health insurance (Medicaid) records tracked 8,996 people for 6 months after they stopped Suboxone's main drug, buprenorphine. All had been on it 6 to 18 months, so the figures may not fit people who stop sooner.

464 had at least one overdose treated by a doctor (5 in 100). 41 to 49 in 100 went to an emergency department, 11 to 14 in 100 stayed in hospital and 19 to 26 in 100 filled a prescription for another opioid.

People who'd been on it 15 to 18 months had fewer emergency visits, hospital stays and opioid prescriptions afterwards than those who stopped at 6 to 9 months, but no fewer overdoses. That's a link, not proof of a cause.
Anyone who died or lost Medicaid in those 6 months was left out, and the records don't say why people stopped. Deaths during and after treatment are in a separate answer.

how: One expert review sums up: after one use, most drugs showed in urine for 1.5 to 4 days, in blood for 1 to 2 days and in saliva for up to 2 days.

Each figure came from one small study, often measured to a lab's lowest limit. Another chart came from textbooks, older reviews and lab websites. The limit matters: one dose of meth showed for 87 hours on average at a lab's limit, 43 at a higher cutoff.
After heavy use, drugs can show up longer than charts say. Among 63 men described as dependent on heroin, 45 in 100 still tested positive for morphine after 6 days. One chart lists 2 days for heroin.

On a locked ward where nobody could smoke, 60 regular weed smokers were tested for up to 30 days. 13 of the 20 with the highest levels were still positive when testing ended. Positives often came back after a negative.
